anomaly_def.Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, work areas, and other engine heaps drives the database process beyond the physical-memory envelope, provoking paging, swapping, or OOM events.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Generation, flushing, or archival of write-ahead log records becomes the principal bottleneck on the write path, inflating commit latency and stalling forward progress when log space or bandwidth is exhausted.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes saturate host CPUs, keeping run queues full and starving other components of compute cycles, thereby inflating response times across the workload.

When these three conditions co-exist, the platform experiences a multilayer resource crisis. Memory pressure forces the engine and operating system to page frequently, which inflates CPU time spent in kernel mode and raises contention on memory latches. Simultaneously, the log subsystem cannot flush or archive fast enough, so commit and checkpoint waits accumulate. Because every commit now lingers on log I/O, client sessions remain active longer, holding onto memory allocations and consuming additional CPU while spinning on log-related waits. The prolonged session lifetimes and retry storms further expand plan and buffer caches, aggravating the memory shortfall, and the elevated CPU utilization slows both log-writer threads and page-reclaimer daemons, creating a feedback loop that deepens stalls. Symptoms therefore blend: escalating commit latency, soaring CPU load averages, runaway RSS growth, swap storms, and ultimately node eviction or crash recovery triggered by failed commits or OOM kills.

Causally, high redo generation drives the log subsystem to its limits; stalled commits elongate transaction lifetimes, which in turn prevent memory buffers from being released and keep worker threads runnable, pushing CPU toward saturation. The CPU bottleneck then slows log flushing and memory reclamation, while memory scarcity induces additional CPU overhead through paging and spin-lock contention. Each anomaly reinforces the others, turning what might have been isolated pressure points into a systemic failure that degrades throughput for write-intensive OLTP workloads and risks abrupt service interruption.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time after which a TCP keepalive message that has not been acknowledged by the client should be retransmitted.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP keepalive probe is not acknowledged for tcp_keepalives_interval on systems supporting TCP_KEEPINTVL or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Controls retry timing for keepalive probes used to detect unresponsive client connections.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
